 CLAS12 analysis note: Neutron Detection Efficiency of the
 Forward Calorimeter using RG-A pass 2 Datasets
 Your names and group number
                                        September 22, 2025

 Abstract
 This analysis note details the steps performed to extract the neutron detection efficiency
 of the CLAS12 forward calorimeter using RG-A pass 2 datasets. The datasets used for this
 analysis were taken in 2018 and 2019, with a 10.6 and 10.2 GeV electron beam scattering on a
 liquid hydrogen target. The results of this study will be used for neutron magnetic form factor
 measurements, Gn  M , in Run Group B and are also essential for other analyses and run groups.

1 Introduction
This note will discuss the method used to calculate the neutron detection efficiency (NDE) in the
forward calorimeter of the CLAS12 detector. This discussion will include the datasets used, the way
of selecting a good neutron, and the cuts applied to these datasets. Additionally, the note will cover
the fitting techniques to extract the NDE results and the parametrization of the NDE results.

2 Method of measuring NDE
The method of measuring the efficiency involves using a hydrogen target to produce tagged neutrons
from the reaction p(e, e′ π + )n. We can determine the tagged neutron missing momentum, Pmm , by
identifying both the scattered electron and the π + detected in the CLAS12 Forward detector and
assuming the missing particle is a single neutron. Once we know the neutron missing momentum,
we check to see if it will strike the fiducial region of the CLAS12 calorimeters. That is done by
calculating the neutron’s path, which is a straight line starting from the electron vertex position, and
continuing to an intersection point with either the pre-shower calorimeter (PCAL) or electromagnetic
calorimeter (EC inner/ EC outer). If the missing neutron’s calculated path intersects with the
calorimeters, we call it an expected neutron. Otherwise, we skip the event. If we do count an
expected neutron, we then loop over all neutral particle hits in the calorimeters to find a detected
neutron near the path of the expected neutron. With appropriate kinematic cuts that are presented
in Sec. 7.2, we can confirm that we have the detected neutron. This method is illustrated in Fig. 1
where the paths of expected and detected neutron are shown as green and blue lines, respectively.
The intersection points of expected and detected neutrons with the front face of the calorimeters
are shown as green and gray points, respectively. The ratio of the number of detected to expected
neutrons gives us the neutron detection efficiency ϵ:
 Ndetected
 ϵ= . (1)
 Nexpected

 1

Figure 1: The front face of the calorimeter with 6 sectors on the left, and on the right is a close-up
view of the struck sector. The black point shows the electron vertex, the blue point shows the
detected neutron measured by the calorimeter, and the gray and green points show the detected and
expected neutron intersecting with the front face of the calorimeter. The blue line is the detected
neutron’s path, which is calculated from the electron vertex in direction of the blue point while the
green line is the expected neutron’s path starting from the electron vertex and moving in direction
of the missing momentum of the neutron.

3 Datasets Used
To extract the neutron detection efficiency (NDE), we first identify and select the exclusive ep →
e′ π + (n) events from the RG-A pass 2 dataset. The dataset was processed through the ePiNCND
train, and at the time of writing, the files are available at the following locations:

 • Fall 2018 inbending:
 /cache/clas12/rg-a/production/recon/fall2018/torus-1/pass2/main/train/ePiNCND/
 *

 • Fall 2018 outbending:
 /cache/clas12/rg-a/production/recon/fall2018/torus+1/pass2/train/ePiNCND/*
 • Spring 2019 inbending:
 /cache/clas12/rg-a/production/recon/spring2019/torus-1/pass2/dst/train/ePiNCND/
 *

The analyzed datasets of RG-A pass 2 were taken during Fall 2018 and Spring 2019 with two different
beam energies 10.6 GeV and 10.2 GeV, respectively. The target used is unpolarized hydrogen (LH2).
The beam current ranges from 40 nA to 75 nA. The torus magnet was set with two different polarities:
outbending, where the track of a negative particle bends away from the beamline, and inbending,
where the track of a negative particle bends toward the beamline. Each dataset was analyzed
separately, as summarized in Table 1.

4 Event Selection
We are interested in the exclusive ep → e′ π + (n) reaction. Events with two charged particles, one
electron and one pion, detected in the Forward Detector were selected. The identification of both
electron and pion follows the procedure described in the PID refinements for RG-A pass 2 note[1].

5 Electron Particle ID
Initially, the electron was selected based on the standard CLAS12 Event Builder (EB) PID =11.
The Event Builder assigns an electron ID to tracks with responses in the HTCC and ECAL that
satisfy the criteria in Table 2.

 Cut Limits
 Charge -1
 Number of Photoelectrons Nph > 2
 Minimum PCAL Energy Deposited Edep > 0.06 GeV
 Sampling Fraction vs. Edep ±5σ

 Table 2: EB electron (PID = 11) assignment requirements.

The following cuts were applied to improve the electron selection criteria.

5.1 Electron Vertex Cut
The 5 cm long LH2 target was placed 3 cm upstream of the CLAS12 center for an inbending torus
field and 5 cm upstream for an outbending torus field. Electrons that originated within the hydrogen
target were selected by applying cuts on the electron vertex position in each of the six sectors, as
shown in Fig. 2. The cut used is based on the PID refinements for RG-A pass 2 note [1]; -8 cm
< vz < 2 cm for the inbending torus and -11 cm < vz < 1 cm for the outbending torus field. The
cut is used to reject electrons that were scattered in the window of the target cell.

5.2 PCAL Fiducial Cut
The fiducial region is the area inside the calorimeter that is considered reliable for making measure-
ments. It is defined as the area away from the edges or boundaries of the calorimeter. The purpose

5.3 DC Fiducial Cuts
Similarly, drift chamber (DC) regions where the electron trajectory is close to the edge of the chamber
volume are removed. The DC fiducial cuts are defined based on the behavior of the track χ2 /NDF
as a function of the distance to the chamber edge (referred to as the edge variable). These cuts were
optimized individually for each particle type, each of the three DC regions, and each datasets.
 Studies of the χ2 /NDF distributions using both data and simulation showed a consistent increase
near the chamber edges. Cut values were determined at the onset of this rise and were found to be
independent of the sector.
 Additional details on the procedure, MC comparisons, and the applied cut parameters can be
found in the RG-A Pass 2 note [1]. Figure 4 shows the DC fiducial cuts for three regions of the DCs
for each dataset.

5.4 Calorimeter Cuts
The sampling calorimeters can be used to differentiate between pions and electrons. Electrons and
pions deposit their energy in the calorimeter differently. Electrons interact in the EC producing
electromagnetic showers and release all of their energy, Edep , which is proportional to their momen-
tum, Pele . On the other hand, charged pions are minimum ionizing particles, which means that
regardless of their momentum, they deposit a constant and small amount of energy. The sampling
fraction (SF) cut can be used to separate electrons and pions. The SF is defined as the ratio of the
total deposited electron energy in all three calorimeter layers (PCAL+EC) to their momentum and
given by:
 Edep ∝ Pele ⇒ Edep /Pele = constant = SF, (2)
where SF is determined by the detector and is around ≈0.25 for electrons for CLAS12 at all momenta,
see Fig. 5. The event builder has a default cut of the sampling fraction as a function of the total
deposited energy of the electron Edep . This cut has a ±5σ limit on the range of the sampling fraction
is shown by the distributions in Fig. 5. In order to improve pion rejection, the sampling fraction
has been divided into electron momentum bins and fitted with Gaussian function in each bin to

 5

determine the mean and sigma per bin. The mean µ and sigma σ of the SF distribution for each
Pele bin are fitted using the following forms:
 !
 Pele 2
 µsf = p0mean · 1 + p 2 + p2mean · Pele + p3mean · Pele ,
 Pele + p1mean (3)
 p1sigma 2
 σsf = p0sigma + √ + p2sigma · Pele + p3sigma · Pele ,
 Pele
where pimean and pisigma (i = 0, 1, 2, 3) are fit parameters that depend on the momentum bin and
sector, as described in [1]. A cut of µ ± 3.5σ was applied from Ref. [1] and as shown by the red,
upper, and lower curves in Fig. 5.

 In addition to the total sampling fraction cut, a two dimensional cut was applied based on the
correlation between the sampling fractions of the inner calorimeter (EECin /pele ) and the PCAL
(EPCAL /pele ) to further improve pion rejection. As shown in the top panel of Fig. 6, electron events

 6

form a nearly linear band, while pion contamination appears mostly below and to the left of this
band.
 To reduce this contamination, the electron band was divided into small momentum slices. Each
slice was fitted to extract the mean and sigma of the distribution, and a cut was applied at the mean
minus two times the most probable σ value, taken as 0.026 GeV. This procedure was performed
independently in eight momentum bins (1 GeV wide) and for each of the six sectors. More details
on the slicing procedure, momentum binning, and cut parameters can be found in the RG-A Pass 2
note [1].
 An additional cut requiring EPCAL /pele > 0.05 was applied to remove low-energy pion contami-
nation, as this region contains very few electrons. See the red line in the top row of Fig. 6. The effect
of this two-dimensional cut is shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 6. All cuts applied for identification
electron are summarized in Table 3.

6 π + Particle ID
6.1 Vertex Difference Cut
To reject pions produced outside of the target region a cut on the difference between the reconstructed
electron z-vertex position and the pion vertex is applied. A loose cut of |vz (ele) − vz (π + )| < 20 cm
is placed for all three different datasets, as shown in Fig. 7. The cut used is based on the RG-A
pass2 note [1].

of the π + to the FTOF(L):

6.3 Fiducial cuts for DC
The drift-chamber fiducial cuts for positive pions have been applied based on the behavior of the
track χ2 /NDF as a function of the edge variable, similar to the cut for electrons. The result of
this cut in the three drift chamber regions is shown in Fig. 9. More details of the DC fiducial cuts
including the exact parametrizations can be found in the RG-A pass2 note [1]. The summary of the
cuts applied for identification of pion is shown in Table 4.

7.1 Identification of the reaction p(e, e′ π + )n
Once a scattered electron and a π + have been identified, the missing mass and missing momentum
of the p(e, e′ π + )n reaction can be calculated by considering 4-momentum conservation:
 Peµ + Ppµ = Peµ′ + Pπµ+ + Pmm
 µ
 , (8)

where P µ =(P⃗ , E) for each particle and Pmm
 µ
 =(P⃗mm , Emm ) is the missing neutron 4-momentum.
The 3-momentum vector P⃗e of the incoming electron is zero in the x and y directions (beam moves
along z-axis) and the 3-momentum vector P⃗p of the target proton is zero (initially at rest). The
missing mass can be calculated as
 P µ mm Pµ mm = E 2 mm − P 2 mm = M M 2 . (9)

                                                                                         Pxmm = −Pxe′ − Pxπ+ ,                                                                                                     (11)

 To identify the expected neutron p(e, e′ π + )n, we swim the neutron through the CLAS12 detector
to the calorimeter. The neutron’s path is a straight line starting from the electron vertex position and
pointing in the missing 3-momentum direction. If the neutron’s path intersects with the calorimeters,
it counts as an expected neutron. If the intersection point lies outside the calorimeters, the event is
dropped. An additional fiducial cut is applied for the expected neutron to be more than 10 cm from
the edge of the calorimeters. The fiducial cut is defined by rotating x − y of the expected neutron
by (s − 1)60◦ where s is the sector number as shown in the upper plots of Fig. 12. Bottom plots in
Fig. 12 show the result of the fiducial cut in all sectors.

7.2 Identification of the reaction p(e, e′ π + n)
Once the expected missing neutron is identified a tight M M cut on the expected missing neutron
is applied to select the actual neutron measured in the calorimeter. The cut used on the expected
neutron corresponds to a 2σ cut on the Gaussian as shown in Fig. 13.

the expected neutron with the direction of the detected neutral particles. The detected neutral hit

                                               #p(e, e′ π + n)
 ϵ= (22)

Below is the summary of the cuts applied to the expected and the detected neutrons:
1) Expected neutron events p(e, e′ π + )n:
 • Intersect with the face plane of the calorimeters.

 • Pass fiducial cuts.
 2) Detected neutron events p(e, e′ π + n):
 • All cuts listed in Tables 3 and 4.

 • The difference in direction cosines,

9 Background Subtraction
Generally, the neutron efficiency is calculated as a function of the missing momentum, Pmm . The
procedure we used to extract the neutron yield involves fitting the missing-mass distribution of both
expected and detected neutrons at different Pmm bins with two different functions: (1) a Gaussian
with a fourth-order polynomial for the background and (2) a Crystal Ball function with a fourth-
order polynomial.

9.1 Gaussian and a fourth-order polynomial
The missing mass distributions of expected and detected neutrons were analyzed using a combined
model composed of a Gaussian function to represent the neutron peak and a fourth-order polynomial
to describe the background. The procedure was applied to each Pmm bin as follows:

 1. The missing mass distribution is binned into 36 Pmm values for both expected and detected
 neutrons.
 2. A Gaussian function is used to model the neutron peak:
 (x−µ)2
                                            fG (x) = A e− 2σ2                                     (23)

 where A is the amplitude, x is the missing mass (M M ), µ is the mean, and σ is the standard
 deviation of the Gaussian.
 3. A fourth-order polynomial is used to model the background contributions:

                                 P ol(x) = P0 + P1 x + P2 x2 + P3 x3 + P4 x4                      (24)

 where Pi are the polynomial coefficients.
 4. The combined fit function is given by:

                                           F (x) = fG (x) + P ol(x)                               (25)

 5. An initial fit was performed for each Pmm bin, starting from the same set of parameters and
 allowing all of the parameters of the Gaussian and polynomial functions to vary freely for both
 the expected and detected neutron distributions. This procedure provides two sets of mean
 (µ) and width (σ) values: one for the expected neutron distribution and one for the detected
 neutron distribution. The results from fitting for this step for selected Pmm bins are shown
 in the first column of Figs. 18, 19, and 20 for the inbending 10.6-GeV dataset. These figures
 show the fits for three representative Pmm bins, corresponding to low, middle, and high missing
 momentum ranges. A complete set of results for all the Pmm bins is in Appendix A.
 6. From the initial fits, the average Gaussian mean (µavg ) and width (σavg ) were calculated for
 each Pmm bin. Up to this point we have treated the expected and detected neutrons the same
 (same cuts, procedures, etc.). The shape of the Gaussian distribution should be the same
 (equal µ and σ) for each Pmm bin. The number of events is proportional to the amplitude
 which can differ between the expected and detected neutrons.
 7. A second round of fitting was performed using the averaged values µavg and σavg as fixed
 parameters. In this step, only the Gaussian amplitude and the polynomial coefficients were
 allowed to vary. The fitting of this step is shown in the second column of Figs. 18, 19, and 20.

 16

 8. To further optimize the fits, a third refinement step was applied using a grid search method:
 • A grid of candidate (µ, σ) values was defined around the averaged parameters: µavg ±0.005
                                                                     and σavg ± 0.002.
 • For each (µ, σ) pair in the grid:
 – The combined fit was applied to both the expected and detected histograms.
 – The χ2 values for each fit were calculated.
 – The total χ2 was calculated as the sum of the expected and detected values.
 • The (µ, σ) pair that minimized the total χ2 was selected for the final fit. This fitting is
 shown in third column of figures 18, 19, and 20.

 9. The neutron yield is extracted by integrating the Gaussian function.

 The values of χ2 obtained from the fits optimized by minimizing the total χ2 for the expected
and detected neutron distributions as a function of missing momentum Pmm are shown in Fig. 21.
Among all datasets, the detected neutrons in the inbending 10.6 GeV dataset show the lowest average
χ2 /ν = 4.05, indicating the best overall fit quality. The expected neutrons for the same dataset also
show good agreement, with an average χ2 /ν = 5.64. A similar performance is observed for the
detected neutrons in the inbending 10.2 GeV dataset, with an average χ2 /ν around 5.5. However,
the expected neutron distribution in the inbending 10.2 GeV data shows a moderately higher average
χ2 /ν ≈ 8.25.
 In contrast, the outbending 10.6 GeV dataset yields significantly higher χ2 /ν values for both
expected and detected neutrons (χ2 /ν = 27 and 13 respectively, reflecting poorer fit quality in this
dataset. In all datasets, χ2 /ν values tend to decrease as Pmm increases, indicating that the fit
quality generally improves at higher missing momentum.

Figure 21: The χ2 distributions obtained from the fits optimized by minimizing the total χ2 , as a

 Figure 22 shows the mean and width values of the expected and detected neutron distributions
obtained from the total χ2 minimization using the Gaussian fit function for the three datasets. The
left panel shows the mean values of the neutron peaks for the Pmm bins. Ideally, the neutron peak
is expected to be centered around 0.939 GeV. For both inbending datasets, the extracted mean
values remain relatively stable in the full range Pmm , with the red and green curves between 0.938
and 0.945 GeV. This indicates a consistent and well-centered signal peak for all Pmm bins in these
datasets.
 In contrast, the outbending 10.6 GeV dataset (blue) shows a noticeable variation in the extracted
mean values, with an upward shift at Pmm < 3 GeV, followed by a decline at higher Pmm values.
This variation is likely due to imperfections in the calibration parameters.
 Momentum corrections for electrons and pions, developed by the RG-A group, have been applied
to all three datasets. At this stage, these corrections appear to be effective primarily for the 10.6 GeV
inbending dataset.
 Overall, the results indicate that the inbending datasets provide more reliable and stable neu-
tron peak positions compared to the outbending dataset, which may require further calibration or
refinement to achieve similar precision.
 The right panel of Fig. 22 shows the width (σ) of the neutron signal as a function of missing
momentum Pmm for the three datasets. Overall, the width increases smoothly from one Pmm bin
to the next for all datasets. The two inbending datasets (10.6 GeV and 10.2 GeV) show similar

 19

behavior, with closely matching width values over the entire Pmm range. In contrast, the outbending
10.6 GeV dataset shows a different behavior: its width is narrower than that of the inbending datasets
for Pmm < 2 GeV, but becomes noticeably broader at higher Pmm . For the last three bins at high
Pmm , the width values were estimated by fitting the width distribution below Pmm < 4 GeV with
a linear function and extrapolating the results to determine the corresponding values.
 The fit parameters of the expected and detected neutron distributions obtained using three dif-
ferent approaches—(i) fits with all parameters free, (ii) fits using averaged parameters µavg and σavg ,
and (iii) fits optimized via total χ2 minimization based on Gaussian fits for the three datasets—is
shown in Appendix A.

9.2 Crystal Ball and a fourth-order polynomial
The Crystal Ball (CB) function combines a Gaussian function with a power-law times an exponential
tail on the right side (high-missing-mass side) and is given by:
 1 x−µ 2 x−µ
                                   fCB (x) =Amp e− 2 ( σ )                             for       > −a
 σ
                                              n                             −n                                                                                                                                               (26)
                                               n       |a|2    n          x−µ            x−µ
                                           =       e− 2           − |a| −          for         ≤ −a
                                              |a|             |a|          σ               σ

where Amp, µ, and σ define the amplitude, mean, and width of the Gaussian part of the function,
respectively. The parameter a controls the location of the transition point between the Gaussian
and power-law parts of the function and n determines the steepness of the power-law tail. The CB
function is commonly used to model distributions that have a peak with a tail, especially when the
data show non-Gaussian behavior at the edges of the distribution. This is particularly useful in
cases where detector resolution or radiative effects are significant.
 The primary motivation for using the CB function is that a simple Gaussian function is insuffi-
cient to describe missing mass distributions. These distributions are often distorted due to detector
resolution effects and radiative effects, where the radiative effects are due to electron-target inter-
actions before or after the hard electron-proton scattering leading to low energy photons that are

 20

not accounted for in the M M calculation. The Crystal Ball function provides a better fit to the
shape of the missing mass distributions, particularly at low missing momentum Pmm bins. The tail
of the CB function is investigated using the semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) Monte
Carlo (MC) simulation. The SIDIS MC is generated using the clasdis generator, which is based on
the LEPTO generator [4]. More details on SIDIS MC can be found in [1]. The tail of the missing
mass distribution of (e, e′ π + n) for inbending 10.6 GeV is shown at high missing mass distribution
in Fig. 23. It extends to a higher missing mass.

Figure 23: The missing mass distribution of p(e, e′ π + n) for inbending 10.6 GeV, generated from
SIDIS MC.

 The fitting procedure for the missing mass distributions of expected and detected neutrons uses
a Crystal Ball (CB) function for the signal component, combined with a fourth-order polynomial
to model the background. This approach follows the same methodology described earlier in Section
9.1 for the Gaussian fits, with the following modifications.

 • In Step 6, the average tail parameters aavg and navg , along with µavg and σavg , were extracted
 for each Pmm bin.
 • In Step 7, these averaged values (µavg , σavg , aavg , navg ) were fixed, and only the CB amplitude
 and polynomial coefficients were allowed to vary.
 • In Step 8, a grid search was performed over (µ, σ, a, n) around the averaged values, and the
 combination that minimized the total χ2 was selected for the final fit.

 The CB function provides improved fitting performance compared to the Gaussian model, espe-
cially in the low Pmm region. Figures 24, 25, and 26 show the fits for three representative Pmm bins,
corresponding to low, middle, and high missing momentum ranges.
 The fits of the expected and detected neutron distributions were obtained using the same three
steps as in Section 9.1; (1) fits with all parameters free, (2) fits using averaged parameters µavg
and σavg , and (3) fits optimized via total χ2 minimization. The results are shown in Appendix B.
These fits were performed using the Crystal Ball (CB) for the signal component combined with a
fourth-order polynomial for the background for 36 Pmm bins for each of the three datasets.

 Figure 27 shows the χ2 values obtained from the CB fits optimized by minimizing the total
 2
 χ for both expected and detected neutron distributions. For the expected-neutron, inbending,
 10.6-GeV dataset, the CB function provides a slightly better fit, with lower χ2 /ν values compared
 to the Gaussian function (χ2 /ν values of 3.8 versus 5.6). A comparable level of improvement is
 also observed in the expected, inbending, 10.2-GeV dataset (χ2 /ν values of 4.2 versus 8.3). In the
 expected, outbending 10.6-GeV dataset, the improvement is more significant: for expected neutrons
 the reduced χ2 decreases from approximately χ2 /ν ≈ 27 (Gauss) to approximately χ2 /ν ≈ 17 (CB),
 while the reduction for detected neutrons is smaller. We observe similar trends for the detected
 neutron results. Compare Figs. 21 and 27. Overall, the CB function results in a better fit quality
 than the Gaussian function, especially at low missing momentum.
 The extracted mean (µ) and width (σ) values from the CB fits for the expected and detected
 neutron distributions show similar behavior to those obtained from Gaussian fits. A complete set of
 fit parameters for each dataset is provided in the Appendix B.
 The comparison of the number of neutron signals extracted from the fits optimized by minimizing
 the total χ2 using the Gaussian and CB polynomial fitting functions for the three datasets is shown
 in Fig. 28. The left panel shows the number of expected neutrons, while the right panel shows the
 number of detected neutrons, both plotted as functions of the missing momentum Pmm . For all
 three datasets, the CB function yields consistently higher neutron signal counts compared to the
 Gaussian function. This difference arises because the CB function accounts for the asymmetric tail in
 the distribution, leading to improved signal extraction. A detailed comparison of the fit parameters
 obtained using the Gaussian and CB functions for each dataset is provided in Appendix C.

10 NDE Results
Once the missing mass of expected and detected neutrons are fitted in each missing momentum bin
Pmm , the yields of the neutron signal can be calculated by integrating either Gaussian or Crystal
Ball function. The detection efficiency in each momentum bin can be calculated as:
 Ndeti
 ϵi = , (27)
 Nexp i

where ϵi is the efficiency in the ith missing momentum bin, Ndeti is the yield of the detected neutron
signal in the ith missing momentum bin, and Nexp i is the yield of the expected neutron signal in
the ith missing momentum bin. An uncertainty to the efficiency in the ith bin is calculated based
on the binomial distribution s
 ϵi (1 − ϵi )
 σi = . (28)
 Nexp i − 1
A comparison of the neutron efficiency calculated by the Gaussian function and the Crystal ball
function, binned in missing momentum of the neutron, is shown in Fig. 29. The comparison is
shown for each datset individually, inbending and outbending 10.6 GeV, and inbending 10.2 GeV.

 24

The agreement between the two functions is striking over all missing momentum Pmm bins. The
difference between the two functions is within 3% as shown in Fig 30. Figure 31 shows the results, of
the present analysis, for the CLAS12 neutron detection efficiency compared to the CLAS6 data. The
CLAS12 results show that all three datasets, inbending and outbending 10.6 GeV and inbending 10.2
GeV, are consistent to each other in both functions. The CLAS12 results are a higher compared to
the CLAS6 result over all Pmm bins because of the additional PCAL detector. The efficiency result
of the CLAS12 data increase with increasing the missing momentum of the neutron, and plateaus
at about 77%, while the plateaus of the CLAS6 at about 60%.

11 NDE parameterization
In order to use the NDE results for GnM in our analysis codes, we need a functional form that can
describe these results. The neutron detection efficiency as a function of the missing momentum,
Pmm , is fitted using a least-squares method with the following function:

 η(Pmm ) =a0 + a1 Pmm + a2 Pmm 2 + a3 Pmm 3 for Pmm < pt
 !
 1 (29)
 =a4 1 − Pmm −a5 for Pmm ≥ pt ,
 1 + exp a6

 26

where a0 , a1 , a2 , a3 , a4 , a5 , a6 and pt are the parameters of the fit. The boundary between the two
parts of the fitting, pt , is varied in the fit. The uncertainty of the fit at a given missing momentum
can be calculated from the error matrix:
 X ∂η ∂η
                                                                        ση 2 =          ϵij           ,                                                                         (30)
 i,j
 ∂ai ∂aj

where η is the value of the fitted function, ai and aj are the ith and j th parameters of the fit,
respectively, and ϵij is the value of the error matrix.
 The fits and associated uncertainties are shown in Fig. 32 for a Gaussian function in the top and
for a Crystal Ball function in the bottom. The black line shows the fit for the NDE result using
the functions in Eq. 29. The right plots in Fig. 32 show the band of the uncertainty on the fits for
both Gaussian (top) and Crystal Ball functions (bottom). The bottom plot in each panel shows the
residuals, which lie close to zero as expected. Table. 5 summarizes the parameters of the fit results
for the two functions.

 Since two different functional forms are used to determine the Neutron Detection Efficiency
(NDE), the difference between the resulting parameterizations can be considered a measure of the
systematic uncertainty.
 Figure 33 shows a comparison of the NDE as a function of the missing mass Pmm , based on
two sets of fit parameters obtained from Gaussian and Crystal Ball (CB) models, respectively. The
left panel shows the NDE curves corresponding to each model: the Gaussian result is shown in
blue, while the CB result shows in red. The the fits closely match over most of the range; however,
small discrepancies appear around the transition point pt . The right panel shows the point-by-point
difference between the Gaussian and CB parameterizations. The difference shows oscillations near
the transition region and then decreases toward zero at higher values of Pmm , indicating that both
fitting functions introduce only a small systematic effect on the NDE extraction.

Chapter 1.

Introduction

Precis and LRID Reflection

1.1 History of the Jefferson Lab

 The Thomas Jefferson Lab (JLAB) is a US Department of Energy-funded National

laboratory in Newport News, Virginia. The history of the laboratory culminates many

interests proposed by the Nuclear Science Advisory Committee (NSAC) “Long Range

Plan” [1] in 1979. It called for a new accelerator facility that satisfied multiple interests

within the community: It was argued that an accelerator facility with a high duty factor

(~100%) and operation luminosities of 1035 cm-2s-1 [13] could allow for continuous

acceleration of energies greater than 2GeV, stating that this would be significant enough

energy to probe internal nucleon structure. A continuous beam satisfied the conditions to

perform exclusive and semi-inclusive measurements, making coincidence experiments

possible [1]. These specifications enable interactions between scattered products to be

 8

identified, providing deeper studies into elastic and inelastic scattering [2][13]. Facilities

such as The Stanford Linear Accelerator Facility (SLAC) could perform acceleration at

sufficient energies to investigate this scattering but with current accelerator limitations.

SLAC had a lower kinematic range due to the accelerator’s linear structure, and could

only operate in short bursts, as its low-duty (<1%) factor Linac Cavities would melt under

continuous applied current. By 1973, the SLAC group had performed 8 major experiments

[3] which gave insight into deep inelastic e-p, e-d, and e-n scattering which reached the

limit of the current day accelerators. This confirmed the existence of a quark structure,

and the limits of the physics possible with existing accelerator facilities, contributing to

NSAC’s proposition. In 1987, construction of the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator

Facility (CEBAF) - which later became JLab – began, at a beam energy of 4GeV. Since its

activation in 1995, the laboratory has performed hundreds of experiments in its four

experimental halls. In 2012, CEBAF ceased operation in preparation to upgrade from

6GeV energy maximum to 12GeV. One major modification from this increase is the

upgrade of CLAS in Hall B allows physicists to take advantage of the 12GeV beam energy.

The upgrades were completed in December 2017, and the facility has been operated

continuously, for approved and ongoing experiments ever since.

1.2 Physics at CEBAF

 In the time around the proposition of the 1979 Long-Range Plan, a new theory for

Nuclear Strong Interaction known as Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) had been

developed. In Color Theory, Color-carrying “flux tubes” connect gluons and determine

their interactions. Color confinement describes quarks as color-carrying constituents that

 9

cannot be observed individually and must be confined to color-neutral Hadrons. Non-

perturbative QCD correctly models color confinement, as it describes interacting particles

as “single-bound states of permanently confined constituents called quarks” [4], that

carry electric charge, with gluons interactions between quarks. Asymptotic freedom is a

feature of QCD, describing how at higher four-momentum Q2 (multi-GeV), quarks

interact weakly [25]. Higher momentum allows us to probe short-distance measurements

due to a low uncertainty, and a lower incident electron de Broglie wavelength, at which

point quarks behave as free particles. This free state would allow for greater observation

of the prediction of quark color and quark confinement [4][5]. The discovery of

asymptotic freedom was important enough to receive the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physics.

JLab was built with the intent to observe the transition from hadronic degrees of freedom

to quark-gluon degrees of freedom. However, it has proved difficult to accurately observe

this, so entirely new tools had to be developed to image the nucleon interior. A Higher

kinematic range, and fully exclusive measurements would provide optimal conditions for

observing and extending this transition, and current QCD distributions [6], allowing for

high Q2 form factor measurements. JLab was originally built with lower energy because

we expected to see the transition from hadronic degrees of freedom (protons, neutrons,

pions) to quark-gluon ones. That transition has proven hard to pin down, but we have

developed a whole new set of tools for imaging the nucleon interior.

 10

1.3 Nuclear Form Factors

 At lower energies, the Elastic and Magnetic form factors can describe the spatial

distribution of charge, current, and magnetization within nucleons. These form factors

provide insight into the scale of nucleon internal structure and the total contributions

from each constituent quark [18]. Form Factors encode the momentum distributions of

the charge and magnetization of the nucleon, which are then connected to the spatial

distributions of charge and magnetization by Fourier transforms. The four
 𝑝 𝑝 𝑛
electromagnetic form factors (EEFFs) of the proton (𝐺𝑀 , 𝐺𝐸 ) and neutron (𝐺𝑀 , 𝐺𝐸𝑛 ) at low

energies, are relatively well-understood. However, at higher energies (>4GeV) there are

few agreeable measurements, leading to an ongoing campaign in Halls A and B at JLab to

provide precise measurements of the EEFFs at high Q2 (~10GeV). At JLab, 7 experiments

have been approved to investigate the form factors, where some are still ongoing. The
 𝑛
Jefferson Lab has optimal facilities for extracting the value of 𝐺𝑀 , where one experiment

to measure it is currently approved and is partially completed. The experiment described

here measures the ratio of inelastic electron-neutron (e-n) over electron-proton (e-p)

scattering events and thus requires measuring neutrons, which this study provides

important information towards.

 11

1.4 Accelerator Facility Overview

 CEBAF is a recirculating electron accelerator at JLab, built from the specifications

laid out by NSAC in 1979, running with a ~100% duty factor, allowing for continuous

acceleration with energies up to 12GeV. A comprehensive layout of CEBAF is shown in

Figure 1.41 (See Appendix C for additional plots outlining CEBAF subsystems). A 100keV

photocathode within CEBAF’s electron gun emits electrons, split into 499MHz bunches

by a radio-frequency chopper[12] at an 85% polarization [9]. These bunches are phase

separated by 120 degrees, in preparation for arrival at each of the individual hall’s A, B,

C, and D. This phase separation is important as it allows the beam splitter at the end of

 Figure 1.41: Rendition of the Continuous Electron Beam Accelerator
 Facility (CEBAF). Showing an overview of the general facility structure, a
 picture from [8], hall D has been edited in for fullness.

 12

the acceleration sequence to appropriately send the electron bunches to each hall. The

Electrons are accelerated up to 123MeV within the electron gun and are injected into the

Northern Linac to begin recirculation through CEBAF. Two superconducting

radiofrequency (SRF) Linacs, north and south, provide electron acceleration of up to

12GeV after 5 laps for halls A, B, and C, and 5-1/2 laps for Hall D. Each Linac contains

200 5-cell 1497MHz Niobium cavities, matching the frequency of the electron bunches.

Each cell has a length of βπ/2, where β=v/c, so a magnetic field accelerates electrons

applied each half radio frequency period [10][11]. A 17000-gallon cryogenic refrigerator

circulates liquid helium throughout sets of cryo-modules and cryo-units. Between each

cryomodule is a set of quadrupole magnets that apply a transverse magnetic field to the

electrons, which direct and focus the beam, and assist in maintaining a low halo. This

means the electrons remain tightly concentrated in a well-defined central region within

the beam, which allows for better beam management and targeting, along with protecting

delicate components within the facility. These various corrective procedures are

continuously performed along the Linac, maintaining a high duty factor (~100%), and

continuous acceleration by keeping the cavities at a temperature of 2K[11]. Five arc

magnet layers are positioned between each Linac's poles to recirculate electrons through

the accelerator. Spreading magnets bend electron paths of different energy vertically at

each Linac's ends into arcs of dipole magnetics that transport the beam to the next Linac

pass, at which point they are recombined. The Electrons receive no increase in

momentum through the arcs and all travel at the same speed, independent of energy.

Electrons are recirculated through CEBAF up to five times (five and a half for hall D, see

figure 1.41), reaching a maximum of 12GeV, at which point the beam switchyard allocates

a path to the halls.

 13

1.5 The CLAS12 Detector
 Located in Hall B is the CEBAF Large Acceptance Spectrometer at 12GeV

(CLAS12). Formally known as CLAS in the 6GeV era, it was constructed upon the 12GeV

upgrade in 2016. With a continuous electron beam, the Detector design followed the many

major prospects NSAC proposed for deepening the current understanding of nuclear

physics: Hadron and Meson spectroscopy at CLAS12 allows for greater understanding of

QCD distributions, confinement, alongside studies of higher mass baryon final states and

mesonic states [14]. The Design additionally permits an extension of past and current

 14

Generalized Parton distributions (GPDs), QCD distributions, and form factor data, due to

a higher kinematical range and a greater maximum Q2. The Detector captures most of the

scatter products from an event over a large portion of the 4π solid angle. It is separated

into two major sub-systems surrounding a polarizable target: the Central Detector (CD)

and the Forward Detector (FD), the main components and subsystems of which are shown

in Figure 1.51. (see sections 1.5.1 and 1.5.2 for more information). Two superconducting

magnets; a toroid and a solenoid provide a 5T magnetic field that bends the paths of

particles through CLAS12, and a zero field can additionally be generated around the target

to allow for polarization [15].

1.5.1 Central Detector Overview
 Electrons that are strongly deflected have their scatter products spread over great

angles; these are captured by the Central Detector (CD). The CD surrounds the target,

covering a polar angle of 35º < θ < 135º, with 360º azimuthal angle coverage. This is

provided by the CD’s Central time-of-flight (CTOF) detector [13], and Central Neutron

Detector (CND). These subsystems assist with charged particle identification performed

by subsystems in the Forward Detector (FD) (see section 1.5.2). Tracking in the CD is

performed by the Silicon Vertex Tracker (SVT) and the Barrel Micromegas Tracker

(BMT), combined into what is known as the Central Vertex Tracker (CVT). Furthermore,

a Central Neutron Detector (CND) is placed as the outermost layer to the CD to detect

neutrons and other neutral particles with a ~10% efficiency [20].

 15

Figures 1.52, 1.53 : CTOF (left), adopted from [13], CND (right) additionally showing
the solenoid, adopted from [20]. Figures visualize the polar and azimuthal coverage of
the CD. (See Appendix B, figure B.2 for more geometric information)

1.5.2 Forward Detector Overview
 As electrons retain their forward momentum, most of the scatter products are

weakly deflected by the torus and are captured by the FD. These FD lies farther down the

beamline to capture these scatter products, covering a polar angle of 5º < θ < 45º. A

forward tagger (FT) is used to cover the internal 2.5º < θ < 4.5º. Particles that pass

through the FD are tracked and identified using 6 subsystems: High/ low Threshold

Cherenkov Counters (HTCC/LTCC) and the Forward time-of-flight (FTOF) provide

particle identification and timing information in conjunction with the

Electromagnetic/Pre-shower Calorimeters (ECAL/PCAL), which also measure energy. In

addition, the Ring Imaging Cherenkov Detector (RICH) provides further identification

for heavier charged Pions/Kaons with energies > 3GeV [13]. As particles above this energy

cannot be distinguished by the HTCC and LTCC and cannot be identified because of the

resolution of the FTOF. Drift Chambers (DCs) measure the path that individual charged

particles take through the FD and are pivotal for the final reconstruction.
 16

1.5.3 Particle Tracking and Identification

 Electron collisions with CLAS12’s target create a reaction, where products are

scattered throughout the FD and CD. Each product is tracked and identified from data

processed by each subsystem, and its path through the detector is reconstructed, named

an “event”. The HTCC spans 5-35º over the polar angle [16] and covers the majority of the

azimuthal angle, it is used to identify electrons, pions, and Kaons at low energies (<3GeV).

It utilizes Cherenkov radiation produced by high-speed electrons moving through a CO2

gas medium and focuses the light through a series of 48 mirror panels. This is collected

by light cones into PMTs and processed into a coordinate cluster. Drift Chambers (DCs)

are used to reproduce particle tracks and map particle trajectories through the forward

detector's toroidal magnetic field. There are three regions of six azimuthal sectors, each

region divided into two superlayers containing 6 layers of positive signal wires arranged

in hexagonal cells by layers of negative field wires. A six-dimensional “cross” is placed

between the two superlayers of each of the three DC regions during tracking. A distance

of closest approach (DOCA) method for each hexagonal wire cross-section is employed to

track the path through the superlayers shown in Figures 1.54, and 1.55. This portion of

particle tracking incorporates the drift time of electrons through the chambers and is part

of CLAS12’s Time-Based-Tracking (TBT), (see section 2.1.2). The LTCC plays a similar

role as the HTCC and works in conjecture with it, providing particle identification instead

at greater energies (>3GeV). Two panels within the FTOF identify particles using two-

layer sets of scintillator bars with PMT readout channels. Particles can be recognized

through their Pion/kaon/proton separation thresholds using two panels - 1a and 1b. Panel

1a covers 5º < θ < 35º polar angle at a time resolution of 80ps, with additional coverage

calorimeters (ECAL/PCAL) are positioned at the downstream end of the FD, they

sheets create particle showers in response to interacting with a scattered particle. A

shower is measured by 3 sets of PMT readout channels, culminating in the layered signals

creating a “pixel” on the surface, as seen in Figure 1.57. From this readout, a coordinate

for a particle’s “hit” can be calculated and used for reconstruction.

Chapter 2.

Methodology

2.1 CLAS12 Software Framework

 CLAS12 contains more than 100,000 readout channels from its combined

subsystems, each outputting significant amounts of raw data information, which must be

processed to identify the particles and reconstruct their path through the detector. This

process can be separated into data acquisition and event reconstruction, Figure 2.11

shows this graphically. CLAS12’s reconstruction and analysis processing framework

(CLARA), is the overarching software that provides users with an easily scalable service-

oriented architecture, meaning users can easily access and process information without

the hassle of software development. Within this framework lies CLAS12’s dedicated

reconstruction software named the CLAS Offline Analysis Tools (COATJAVA). This code

provides users with common tools that make navigation and reconstruction more easily

accessible. Additionally, it includes a series of software packages each with direct and

specific functionalities for reconstruction.

 20

2.1.1 Raw Data Acquisition

 Initial raw data processing within CLAS12 goes through three stages to be

processed into a format COATJAVA can analyse. Firstly, the time-to-digital converters

(TDCs) and analogue-to-digital converters (ADCs) process signals into a HIPO format.

This format easily and efficiently stores data into information such as signal strength,

position, and time in the calorimeters and FTOF, or the number of photoelectrons in the

Cherenkov counters [21].

2.1.2 Event Reconstruction Process

 A three-stage Trigger system is used for data collection and is the first step in the

reconstruction process. An initial Global Trigger maps particle locations and trajectories

generated with Geant4 simulations of CLAS12’s geometry, topology, and readout

channels. In Stage 1, the ADC information is collection and events are selected based on

hits and clusters generated by each subsystem. Stage 2 uses information from the TDCs

to match coincidence clusters, timing, and geometry between detectors, and subsystems.

Stage 3 collects the previous trigger bits into a single stream to be sent to the Data-

acquisition-system (DAQ) [22]. Raw data collected by the DAQ is stored in JLab’s Event

Input/Output (EVIO) data format and compressed into a dedicated high-performance

output (HIPO) file type. This file type has special indexing features, allowing the files to

be easily differentiated based on the event particle information. Banks store and sort this

data to then be processed by dedicated algorithms within each detector subsystem.

 21

Firstly, hit-based tracking (HBT) is performed: where tracks are reconstructed based on

hit positions on each subsystem, and information such as particle timing, momentum,

and energy is matched to the track. This is sent through the event builder (EB), which

sorts this information into Reconstruction (REC) banks based on which process it was

generated by, as shown in Figure 2.11. Finally, time-based tracking (TBT) is performed:

where the REC banks are sent back through the EB and are given an event “start time”

[21], which assists with calibrating more accurate tracks and timing information through

the reconstruction process. Additionally, the EB functions as a generalized particle

identifier: allocating and storing information such as three momentum (px, py, pz) and

energy deposited under particle IDs (PIDs) for each particle in an event.

Figure 2.11: Graphical representation of the reconstruction process, showing processing of data
from the Input/output package, through databanks, software packages and finally through the
event builder into relevant reconstruction banks and output files.

 22

2.1.3 Additional Cuts

 Throughout reconstruction, certain cuts are applied to particles in each subsystem

within CLAS12 for optimal data selection, the cuts are taken from [23]. Electron vertex

cuts on the target ensure electrons that scatter outside the target window are discarded.

Photoelectron cuts select any photons within the HTCC and LTCC that produce more than

2 photoelectrons. Fiducial cuts on the Calorimeters ensure hits are within either 9cm,

14cm, or 19cm of the edge of each of the six sectors. These values are chosen as they each

represent one scintillator bar distance from the sector edge, defined as loose, medium,

and tight cuts respectively, with medium cuts being used for photons and loose cuts for

electrons. The Drift Chambers also follow an edge cut, which marks out the fiducial

volume that we extract the tracks from [23].

2.2 Neutron Detection Efficiency

 Neutrons pass through CLAS12 FD largely undetected as they cannot be tracked by

the majority of its subsystems, which are optimized for charge particle detection. These

Neutrons can be detected by the calorimeters (ECAL/PCAL) in the FD. Neutrons are

detected through reconstruction of the particle shower created upon a neutral collision

with the PCAL. This study shows that CLAS12 detects and recognizes neutrons at less than

100% efficiency and that this Neutron Detection Efficiency (NDE) must be measured. The

NDE is calculated from the ratio of expected over-detected neutron hits, given by equation

2.1:

2.2.1 Event Selection

 The Event Builder translates particle information into a final output format named

data summary tapes (DST). In this, physics analysis filters are applied to identify different

final states like e-n or e-p. The reaction chosen to determine the NDE is: 𝑒 − + 𝑝 → 𝑒 ′ +

𝜋 + + 𝑛, this final state is e’π+n, as seen in equation 1. This event choice assumes an

electron colliding with a hydrogen target, producing a scattered electron, positive pion,

and neutron. This reaction suggests that these particles are the only possible products,

and the only neutral hit must be a neutron. Other types of neutral particles such as

photons can mimic the reaction caused by Neutrons, so we have to apply selection cuts to

identify the events of interest. This process works internally by iterating over all events in

a dataset, selecting only events with the PIDs for these particles, and discarding any

events otherwise. This is discussed in more detail in the upcoming section.

2.2.2 NDE Method

 Software tools and methods in COATJAVA allow for the charged products to be

“swum” from the electron vertex (the point at which the electron hits the target) forward

to the hit coordinate on the Calorimeters. As the charged particle momenta is known, a

missing momentum bin for the neutron is calculated (see section 2.3.2). Using this

information, a virtual neutron track is swum and extrapolated from the target vertex, and

 24

the coordinates of the hit on the calorimeter are calculated. If the track does not hit the

ECAL, then the event is dropped. The hit location is labelled an “expected” neutron. We

then search over neutral hits measured in the event, If a hit is found near the predicted

location on the ECAL, the event is labelled as a “detected” neutron.

2.2.3 Difference in Direction Cosine

 To extract detected neutron hits on the calorimeter, a difference in direction cosine

cut is applied, as shown in Figure 2.12. The coordinates are such that the z direction is

perpendicular to the ECAL front plane, so the cut applies the transverse x and y

momentum for each neutral. The Momentum in x and y of detected neutrals within a

region around the expected hit are recorded as detected neutrons A cut is applied around

the central region calculated from equation 2.21 and controlled by the parameters in Table

2.21. The detected neutron event with the smallest value from this cut is selected,

discarding all other hits, this process is repeated for each event.

calculate the missing mass of the neutron using the 𝑒 − + 𝑝 → 𝑒 ′ + 𝜋 + + 𝑛 reaction by

knowing the particle energies, given by equation 2.22:

2.3.1 Other Datasets

 For Extracting the NDE at JLab we use the three datasets shown in Table 2.21,

these are Inbending 10.2GeV, Inbending 10.6GeV, and Outbending 10.6GeV. Inbending

uses the torus magnet with a positive polarity, bending scatter products back toward the

beamline, whereas Outbending reverses the polarity bending scatter products to the

outermost edges of CLAS12. These datasets all require different parameterization, with

Inbending 10.6GeV being the main focus in this study (see section 3.1), with a significant

portion of the comparisons being performed using it. Results from the other datasets have

also been performed (see section 3.2).

 27

2.3.2 Missing Momentum
 To study the evolution of the magnetic form factor as a function of outgoing

momentum, the missing mass spectra are separated into separate Missing Momentum

(Pmm) bins spread from 0.375-7.5GeV. The Data does not reach the maximum 10.2-10.6

GeV (depending on the dataset used from Table 2.21) due to the overlap of quasi-elastic

and inelastic events (See Appendix C.1/C.2 for validation). We use 36 Missing Momentum

bins sorted for CLAS12, each with a varying range of momenta and producing MM spectra

that can be individually fitted.

2.3.3 Extracting the Neutron Signal

 The goal of fitting these spectra is to extract the Neutron signal separate from the

background signal intruding upon the missing mass and reduce inelastic neutron events

and photons that may bypass our cuts and selection criteria. To do this we fit a function

to the MM histograms and extract the total neutron yield this function produces. We apply

a Definite integral within a user-defined range over the neutron peak and measure the

background signal by fitting a polynomial background. By fitting the background as a

separate polynomial from the function, we can summate them and produce separate

signals that can be subtracted. Detected fits are performed separately from Expected fits

as they have differences from the cuts we applied in sections 2.1.3 and 2.2.3 and are

analysed separately to obtain individual yields. We can then compare the expected and

detected yields from equation 2.21 to determine the NDE across the missing momentum

distribution.

 28

 Figure 2.13: Missing Momentum bins 2, 12, and 25, taken from the raw ROOT
 file of Inbending 10.6GeV data, these histograms are used in the function fitting
 in the upcoming sections.

2.4 Histogram Fitting Procedures

 The Core of a Missing Mass spectrum usually follows the characteristic symmetric

“bell-curve” shape of a normal distribution. From this judgment, fitting with a Gaussian

or a Gaussian-like function is appropriate. Currently, the NDE has been fitted with a

Gaussian Function and a Crystal Ball function. This study investigates the comparable

differences between these functions and a Double Crystal Ball Function (see sections

2.4.1, 2.4.2, 2.4.3). From Figure 2.13, we can draw the assumption that the parameters of

a fitted function should vary smoothly and increase with missing momentum, as the

background increases, shifting the signal to higher MM.

 29

2.4.1 Higher order Polynomial Background

 All fits are done with a fourth-order polynomial background as this provides the

minimum number of terms needed (see section 3.1.6). Higher-order polynomials are also

suitable for fitting, as they provide adequate terms, however, too many turns raise the

number of degrees of freedom and can lead to poor results, see section 3.1.6. The Gaussian

Parameters must be obtained before proceeding with more complex functions as they are

the purest form of these parameters before additional terms are introduced (see section

2.4.3)

2.4.2 The Reduced Chi-Squared

 When fitting to histograms, the suitability of the fit depends on the Reduced Chi-

squared statistic, measured as chi-square (χ2) per degree of freedom ν.

The goal when fitting is to obtain the lowest possible reduced chi-square value, as this

 30

proves the “goodness” of the fit. If the reduced chi-square is abnormally large, this

suggests the fit has failed somewhere, or is inaccurate at some point within the fit range

2.4.3 Starting Point - Gaussian Function

 A Gaussian function is the purest fitting procedure possible for extracting the yield

as the only variable parameters are the mean (µ), width (σ), and amplitude. It is used as

no additional systematic uncertainty arises from increasing the function’s complexity

with additional terms. The procedure for fitting a Gaussian is as follows:

  Figure 2.41: Plots at three different missing momenta of fitting the NDE data using a
  Gaussian Function, the top row is expected, and the bottom row is detected. The blue
  line is the Gaussian, the green line is the polynomial background, and the red line is
  the sum of the two.

 31

• Begin with a reasonable starting point for the mean and width parameters,

 the most appropriate being the Neutron missing mass (0.9395MeV). This can

 either be from prior understanding or an initial fit.

• Fit the lowest missing momentum detected neutron bin first, this is for two

 reasons: firstly, the detected bins will be the most accurate to the real neutron

 hit on the calorimeter. Secondly, it contains the least background intrusion,

 and therefore, the purest fit.

• Fit each subsequent detected bin using the previous bin’s fit parameters

 generated as the starting point for the current bin’s parameters. It is important

 to start with the detected bins, as it’s measure neutrons.

• The Parameters must be provided with limits. At this point, it is appropriate

 to provide very wide limits (such as one standard deviation) as this gives the

 fitting procedure more data to fit and characterize the inelastic background.

• After fitting all of the detected bin parameters we take each associated

 detected fit and use each parameter in the expected bins. Alternatively, you

 can reproduce the last steps with each expected bin.

• Again, reasonable limits must be applied, however, it is preferable to use

 tighter limits now that reasonable parameters have already been obtained.

• Look for the reduced chi-squared (χ2), and adjust the parameters mean (µ),

 width (σ), and amplitude until the lowest value for the χ2 between the expected

 and detected bins is produced. This can be done by adjusting limits or

 parameters for each bin, or all bins at once and redoing the fit. Note – the

 expected and detected mean and width parameters must be the same.

 32

2.4.2 Gaussian Parameter Shift

 Figure 2.41 shows 3 expected and 3 detected bins performed using a Gaussian

Function and fourth-order polynomial background. They consistently fit the histograms

in Figure 2.31, however, it becomes apparent that the mean should shift to higher missing

mass as missing momentum increases. The parameters mean (µ), width (σ), and

amplitude vary smoothly, where the mean lies within 0.94-0.96MeV. However, with

increasing missing momentum, the mean was observed to gradually increase away from

the neutron missing mass (0.9395MeV) and the width increased in response. This

observed variation is worse for the Outbending run period and is a result of a higher

systematic uncertainty (see section 9.1 of [23], and page 75 of [22]). The parameters

generated from the Gaussian fit are extracted, and used as the starting points for the

fitting of any Gaussian-like functions, so the Parameterization shown on the plots in

Figures 2.42 and 2.43 must be optimal (see effects of this in section 3.1.3)

 Figure 2.42: Parameters mean (µ), and width (σ) plotted after fitting with the same
 conditions as Figure 2.42, making parameter range loose to reveal expected and
 detected independent parameter shift.

 33

 The comparable background yield from neutron yield at high missing mass in the

expected fits in Figure 2.41 is noticeably larger at the same missing momentum than the

detected bins, suggesting the mean shift is altered for the expected bins. This is observed

in Figure 2.42, where the Gaussian parameter range has been allowed to vary largely,

causing the expected and detected Gaussian parameters to differ by up to 3%. This

difference alone causes the NDE ratio results in section 2.2 to be poor. This is shown by

Figure 2.43, where the originally smooth NDE becomes inconsistent. This does result in

good individual reduced chi-square, however, the results are not usable for the NDE (see

section 3.1.3)

2.4.3 Crystal Ball Function

 The Crystal Ball Function—named after the Crystal Ball Collaboration—was

formulated in 1979 by the Stanford Linear Accelerator Facility (SLAC) group as a viable

function to model lossy effects in high-energy particle physics [27][28]. It consists of a

Gaussian core component with a power-law tail stitched onto either side, at low or high

missing mass.

 This functional form determines whether to fit a Gaussian component (top) or

power-law component (bottom), depending on the location of the tail parameters.

Parameter α determines the point at which the tail attaches to the Gaussian core,

measured in standard deviations from the mean, parameter n is exponent in the power

law tail. Giving the parameter α a negative value places the tail at high MM and using a

positive α value places the tail at low MM. This function is then multiplied by a

normalization factor N; this is typically a corrective value to account for the amplitude of

the fit. Figure 2.41 shows a Crystal Ball Function that is plotted with simple, single integer

tail parameters to show their effects.

2.4.4 Double Crystal Ball Function

 The Double Crystal Ball Function is similar, with the addition of another MM tail

on the other side of the Gaussian core. Equation 2.42 shows that it is mathematically

identical to the Crystal Ball function, with the added variability from two additional tail

parameters αL, and nL, which provide the function with two additional conditions. Due to

this, the Double Crystal Ball Function requires further parameterization of the ith tail for

constants A and B and the overall fit. This function can be in Symmetric or Asymmetric

form or single-sided on either side of the Gaussian (see section 3.1.2). The asymmetric

function is predicted to have a lower chi-squared (χ2) due to having more degrees of

freedom.

2.5 Double Crystal Ball Fitting Procedure

 We use the same histograms to fit the MM data, so fitting with a double crystal ball

function begins with fitting the Gaussian function in section 2.4.2. We retain the Gaussian

parameters mean (µ), and width (σ), and keep them fixed for the Double Crystal Ball

fitting procedure. The amplitude can vary as the tails may alter this slightly, the limits

must allow for the whole range of MM bins (from zero to the highest amplitude). The tail

parameters αL, αR nL, and nR are the additional terms we must account for.

2.5.3 Power-law Tail Parameterization

 Similarly to the Gaussian parameters, from Figure 2.31, we expect the tail terms

to vary smoothly as missing momentum increases as they are attached to the Gaussian

core. Due to this, the fitting procedure is similar and is as follows:

  • Begin with reasonable tail values for the first detected bin, these can be

 assumed from your detected Gaussian parameters mean (µ), and width (σ).

 Provide them with a loose range, allowing ROOT to find suitable parameters.

  • Use the previous bin’s tail parameters as starting points for the next Pmm

 detected bin, repeat this for each Pmm bin.

  • Fit the expected bins by using the detected bin tail parameter values as

 starting points for each parameter in the expected bins, this fitting can be done

 for each Pmm bin individually or for all 36 Pmm bins at once.

 39

 • After obtaining tail parameters for both expected and detected bins, search for

 the reduced chi-square. Refit bins if necessary to produce the lowest reduced

 chi-square value possible for both expected and detected fits. Note – the

 expected/detected tail parameters can differ (see section 3.1.1)

2.5.4 Alternative Fitting Procedures

 In Sections 2.4.2 and 2.4.3, the procedure for fitting the Crystal Ball and Double

Crystal Ball Functions is shown, this method has been used consistently and is found to

be the most appropriate (see [22]). However, there are alternative ways to perform this

fitting which could be accounted for in future applications: forced iterative fitting and

Preparatory background fitting. Force iterative fitting makes use of Python looping

functionalities, where you provide the fit with an array of 36 percentage ranges and iterate

over the full 36 bins. I found this method to be suitable for automating the fitting process,

as although it takes significant time, ROOT eventually finds the most appropriate

parameters, this is explored more in section 3.1.8. Preparatory background fitting is

performed by fitting the polynomial background within its appropriate range before

fitting any functions in the signal region, this can provide the user with a pure background

fit before any effect from fitting functions, which can be more appropriate, see section

3.1.9.

 • Comparing Gaussian parameters between fits

 • Comparing influence of additional parameters / tails / functions on signal

 yield, NDE, and the parameters between functions (CB and DCB)

 3.1 Double Crystal Ball for Inbending 10.6GeV

 Fitting, and comparing the Double Crystal Ball Function to previously

 accomplished NDE fits is the main goal of this study, and in the upcoming sections, these

 results of the fitting are discussed in detail for the Inbending 10.6GeV Dataset,

Figure 3.11: Missing Mass fits for a Double Crystal Ball Function with a fourth-order
polynomial background. The Missing momentum bins have the same properties as Figure 2.41.

 41

3.1.1 Tail Parameter Trends

 As Missing Momentum increases, the tail parameters shift, similarly to the

Gaussian Parameters. We expect this as the tails are dependent on the location and shape

of the Gaussian, from equation 2.42. Additionally, the Gaussian parameter shift (see

section 2.4.2) indicates the tail parameters should also shift by a similar degree,

increasing gradually with missing momentum, this is seen in Figure 3.12.

Figure 3.12: Tail Parameters aL, aR (top), and nL, nR (bottom) plotted as a function
of missing momentum Pmm, the red points are detected neutrons, and the black
points are expected neutrons.

 42

 Parameters aL, and aR, show a clear increasing pattern over the missing momentum

range as we expect, however, they prove to be sporadic and unstable, where their positions

are not smooth in the Pmm range, and ROOT struggles to find the most appropriate

location to place them. The parameters nL, and nR, however, are kept consistent for all fits

when determining the best chi-square, remaining at ~100, and not being varied. ROOT

also does not object to these values and changing them has little effect on the fitting

procedure. It is important to note that, unlike the Gaussian Parameters, it is appropriate

to have different tail parameter values between the expected and detected fits (see section

3.1.3)

3.1.2 Symmetry and Asymmetry

 A Double Crystal Ball function can be symmetric, asymmetric, or single-sided,

which is dependent on the tail parameters chosen. Symmetry – tails determined by aL, aR,

and nL, nR will be the same size on either side of the mean (aL, aR, nL, nR will be the same).

Asymmetry – the tails will be different sizes on either side of the mean (aL, aR, nL, nR can

be different). Additionally, aL and aR can be different or the same for both of these cases,

where either nL or nR will be set to zero, making it a single-sided asymmetric DCB

function. The symmetry chosen can affect the chi-square significantly, where it is

expected that asymmetric fits should have a lower reduced chi-square, as from equations

2.41/2.42 there are more degrees of freedom, this is discussed in section 3.1.4.

 43

3.1.3 Reduced Chi-squared Gaussian Dependence

 The Gaussian parameter locations are one of the main contributors to decreasing

the fit's goodness. As discussed in section 2.4.2, the parameter shift means the expected

and detected cores differ slightly along the missing mass spectra. The chi-square is at its

minimum for each expected and detected fit when the most appropriate values for the

Gaussian parameter are used. However, we must balance the values to be the same

between the expected and detected fits, else we are extracting invalid results for the signal.

 Figure 3.13: True Global minimum reduced-chi-square minima, reached after
 allowing the Gaussian parameters to vary significantly, the fit took 5 iterations over
 each bin, performed using the forced iterative fitting method (see section 3.1.8). The
 Mean of which is shown on the right.

 The Global minima is shown in Figure 3.13, alongside its mean. The reduced chi-

square is at the most appropriate value, proving that these parameters produce the best

MM fit for each expected/detected bin. Although the NDE ratio produced from this fit is

assumed to be invalid as the mean is not the same.

 44

 Figure 3.14 highlights the reduced chi-square results when a three separate

approaches to parameterization is taken. The Expected and Detected values of the optimal

plot (bottom row) are ~2 higher than the global minima.

 Figure 3.14: Reduced chi-square (left) as a function of missing momentum Pmm,
 shown to differ based on slight differences in the Gaussian mean parameter. The
 Bottom row is the final DCB fit used to produce the results in section 3.1.7. All fits
 are done with the same amplitude and width as Figure 2.42.

 45

 The top row of Figure 3.14 shows an average ~1 increase to the chi-square from the

final DCB fit, with only an incremental difference in the mean. The Second plots show a

more extreme case: in this scenario, the mean is fixed at the optimal detected value, hence

the chi-square is 1.92 (roughly the global minima). This is a significant distance from the

optimal expected mean; hence the expected chi-square is 8.28. The optimal balance

around keeping the mean the same between the expected and detected fits is shown on

the bottom row.

 Figure 3.15: Plot for the reduced chi-square of the previously
 fitted Crystal Ball Function with fourth-order polynomial.

 The Final DCB chi-square values of expected = 2.63 and detected = 3.87 (shown

in the bottom row of Figure 3.14) are similar to the CB chi-square shown in Figure 3.15,

indicating the addition of an extra tail marginally increasing the quality of the fits. This,

however, could also be from the slightly different Gaussian parameterization.

 46

3.1.4 Reduced Chi-squared Tail Dependence

 Similarly to the Gaussian Parameters, the tail parameters greatly affect the reduced

chi-square of our fit based on their final values. They have a specific range where they are

appropriate and placing them outside of this range can instead cause a large variation in

the chi-square or cause the fitting procedure to error. This can cause an increase of up to

~12 to the optimal reduced chi-square value in the worst cases. Figures 3.15 and 3.16 use

the same parameters as Figure 3.14 other than aL and aR values.

 Figure 3.15: Reduced chi-square (left) shown to vary based on the position of
 parameters aL and aR (right). Top plots show the effect when tail parameter aL
 is made to equal aR, where expected and detected points are kept equal, bottom
 plots show the effect when the parameter position aL is made to equal aR alone.

 47

  Figure 3.16: Reduced chi-square (left) shown to vary based on the position of
  parameters aL and aR (right). Top plots show the effect when tail parameter AR
  is made to equal aL, where expected and detected points are kept equal, bottom
  plots show the effect when the parameter positions AR is made to equal aL alone.

 The reduced chi-square consistently increases in all of the above cases, where both

tail position and expected/detected points cause an effect. However, the increase is more

significant and more apparent when forcing the parameters to have the same expected

and detected points, as seen in Figure 3.16. This is due to this change forcing the

parameters away from their optimal values, reducing the fit quality, so it is imperative to

adjust the tail parameters to have the most accurate values.

 48

 3.1.5 Universal Signal Increase

 Figure 3.17 shows the total signal produced by each fitting method. The total signal

 changes by a predictable amount as you would assume each tail captures more yield

 within the definite integral. The Crystal Ball shows an average of ~5% more yield than the

 Gaussian and the Double Crystal Ball shows an average of ~23% more yield than the

 Gaussian. The Increase differs between the two, showing that the low MM tail captures

 less background than the high MM tail that is introduced from the Double Crystal Ball

 Function. This is very consistent for low missing momentum, but the difference

 consistently loses effect as missing momentum increases. Figure 3.17 shows the difference

 in signal, so we can imply that the tails are very prevalent at low missing momentum but

 negligible at higher missing momentum.

Figure 3.17: Plots showing the signal extracted from the background, produced by the
definite integral between the ranges given in figure 3.22. Shows that the DCB and CB tails
introduce more signal to the NDE ratio.

 49

3.1.6 Testing Different Order Polynomials

 All previous and current results for fitting the NDE have been performed with a

fourth-order polynomial background, finding that it best represents the background

signal in the missing mass spectrum. However, higher-order polynomials should

provide a sufficient number of turns to accommodate both the signal and background. A

Figure 3.18: DCB with fourth-order polynomial (left) against DCB with fifth order-
polynomial (right). Using the exact same starting parameterization as each other,
described in sections 2.4.2 and 3.4.1.

 50

fifth-order polynomial has been shown against a fourth-order polynomial in the missing

momentum bins, as shown in Figure 3.18.

 The visual quality of the fits remains similar for the fifth-order polynomial

although the fitting process shows consistent errors. The tail parameters are allowed to

vary as usual, they do not change from the fourth-order polynomial results, even with the

extra term. The additional parameter implies a minor increase in the reduced chi-square

of the fits. The expected and detected chi-square do increase marginally, this is shown in

Figure 3.19, omitting a minor increase in the detected chi-square from a bin error.

 Figure 3.20: Reduced chi-square plot generated from a DCB function
 fitted with a fifth-order polynomial background, and the same
 parameterization as Figures 2.42 and 3.12.

 51

 In Addition to the fifth-order polynomial, I have tested using a third-order

polynomial – reducing the number of parameters and the number of turns by one. Using

this order polynomial fits the detected bins with similar accuracy and reduced chi-square

as the fourth order. The expected fit shown in Figure 3.21 however, appears anomalous,

with a reduced chi-square that changes sporadically and jumps back up to a higher value

around the mid-missing momentum region. This is likely from there being an

insignificant number of turns in the polynomial to properly fit the MM spectrum once the

background reaches a certain size, which only occurs after reaching a certain missing

momentum.

 Figure 3.21: Reduced chi-square plot generated from fitting using

all of the Inb10p6 Double Crystal Ball fits. The overall range smoothly increases in size as

the lower limit decreases and the upper limit increases. This change in range is necessary

as it becomes difficult to determine the signal when the background increases

significantly. The points are erratic as they have been manually adjusted to Smoothen out

the ratio in Figure 3.24.

3.1.8 Forced Iterative Fitting

 This alternate method for fitting attempts to reiterate the whole fitting process

automatically, which can assist with locating the optimal parameters. It follows similar

processes to the ones highlighted in sections 2.4.3 and 2.5.3, however after finishing a fit,

we reuse the final parameters in bulk as the parameters of the next fit. This can be done

multiple times, and I used this method to obtain the reduced chi-square global minimum

results shown in Figure 3.13. This method obtains the most optimal chi-square for

independent expected and detected fits, and thus the highest quality MM fits. If

performed during the Gaussian portion of fitting, it is not acceptable to use as a method

as the Gaussian parameters will be different between expected and detected fits. If used

when obtaining the tail parameters it can be an applicable method.

 [FIGURES HERE]

3.1.9 Preparatory Background Fitting

 Preparatory background fitting is the final alternate method I have used, which

utilizes setting unique range limits to encapsulate the background by itself and fit it by

using the regular fourth-order polynomial. Doing this will give us a pure set of polynomial

parameters for the background without any influence from the signal and fitting the

Gaussian and tail parameters. This method results in several issues: firstly, when

returning to a full fit, fixing the polynomial terms to the new values causes consistent

errors in the fitting, whereas implementing them with loose limits results in them

returning to the same as before. Secondly, reverting to the old integral range results in a

missing section of the polynomial, which it must refit, again either resulting in errors or

 56

the same results as before. Additionally, this method is only applicable to low missing

momentum as shown in Figure [][], where the background turns over the MM range, once

the background gets too high the more accurate background fitting becomes obsolete.

 [FIGURES HERE]
